body: This also handles the suggested documentation changes in #119948

I'd like to add an additional catch since we're already at it.
Currently passing an all-zero array (eg. `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]`) will result in `-1` being returned, but without an error thrown. It passes by the regular algorithm and the one that tries to at least get a return value if something went wrong before by just returning the index of the first weight (from the back) that's bigger than `0.0` (Both valid to avoid edge cases for `randf() == 1.0` and floating point imprecision due to extinction)
The all-zero case should be caught separate and vocally though i believe. I would add another check below the array summation for this. I think this doesn't need to be mentioned separately in the documentation, it's emergent behaviour from the existing explanation and doesn't really change behaviour of the function 'cept for the error message.

I hope everything works now. Created a project for testing, if anyone wants a go.
[test_project_rand_weighted_err.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28597112/test_project_rand_weighted_err.zip)

> The all-zero case should be caught separate and vocally though i believe.

I'm not sure I agree with this addition. The `-1` return case is established behavior that can be useful in situations where a weighted result scales and you want no-result in the case that--say--the player fails to hit a lower threshold for "loot credits" or something of the sort. 

The `-1` result and the error result are equally arbitrary, but I believe the former has more utilitarian value.

> The `-1` result and the error result are equally arbitrary, but I believe the former has more utilitarian value.

I can see where this can be an issue, but picking a random element based on a zero-likelihood array is nonsensical, ambiguous by nature (depending on the implementation it could return both `-1` (here) and `0`) and should be called out. If this case could occur in a games logic it should be caught ahead of time; If a user wants to use `-1` as a valid 'no-choice' outcome for their game logic, they shouldn't rely on the API's internal error-fallback code to do so.
Passing an array like `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` is semantically identical to passing an empty array `[]` (there being no valid elements to choose from) which we already catch.
Also, returning `-1` without expressing that it was caused by unexpected inputs will lead to uncaught bugs in code that will be tricky to track down. Especially since `-1` is accepted as an index by GDScript, which makes reasonable implementations, for example the one shown in the documentation, quite risky.
`print(my_array[rng.rand_weighted(weights)])` with `weights` somehow being a zero-array would just result in the last element being picked, the developer being none the wiser to the issue.

We could use a warning instead, though I worry it introduces some inconsistency in how we validate inputs for this function.

> picking a random element based on a zero-likelihood array is nonsensical,

At the moment, an all-zero array always return `-1`, which from a game-dev perspective, I can guarantee a few projects exist out there that utilize that fact for their logic. Imagine I have an array of weights that determine loot a player can get. Doing some action increases some index by some amount. If no action is taken but the enemy is defeated, chances are I'm checking for that `-1` since it's an established outcome. 
I'm just concerned about breaking projects by removing that. Edit: _Though I agree a warning would be good in case someone doesn't know about the -1 since it works as an array index_

I've also been testing the existing logic using a gdscript-translated version and I'm not sure the second loop ever runs... Though maybe I haven't tested enough cases.
```cpp
for (int64_t i = weights_size - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
	if (weights[i] > 0) {
		return i;
	}
}
```

	var continue_done: bool = false
	var weights_size: int = len(WEIGHTS)
	var weights_sum: float = 0.0
	for i: int in weights_size:
		weights_sum += WEIGHTS[i]
	
	var remaining_distance = randf() * weights_sum
	for i: int in weights_size:
		remaining_distance -= WEIGHTS[i]
		if remaining_distance < 0:
			outcomes_gdscript_version[OUTCOMES[i]] += 1
			outcomes_gdscript_version["by first loop"] += 1

	if continue_done: continue
	
	# Does this ever run???
	for i: int in range(weights_size - 1, -1, -1):
		if WEIGHTS[i] > 0:

			outcomes_gdscript_version["by second loop"] += 1

	outcomes_gdscript_version["-1"] += 1
print(outcomes_gdscript_version)

# Implemented version...
for x: int in 100000:
	var rand_weighted_outcome: int = rng.rand_weighted(WEIGHTS)
	if rand_weighted_outcome == -1:
		outcomes_implemented_version[str(rand_weighted_outcome)] += 1

Sorry for the tangent, it was just something related I noticed in my testing.

Well, after thinking again, I think I agree with @PodunkGames: 0-total `rand_weighted` could be interpreted like a `find` without any elements: Just return `-1`, which is the feedback. Since single elements are permitted 0 to have "0" value, why isn't all-0?
The main argument against would be that this destroys the contract of "`rand_weighted` always picks an element", but this is already false because of the error potential - and the user can decide whether `-1` fails loudly or silently by how they handle it.

Either way it's questionable and shouldn't be 'folded in' to this one.
I'd say remove it from the PR again; if you're still interested in this change you should make a follow-up PR with separate discussion.

About breaking projects:
The error code is `-1`, so any project that used the `-1` as a valid return for zero-arrays will still work, the error thrown doesn't stop execution, it only appears in the debugger. Here an output extract from the [test_project_rand_weighted_err.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28597112/test_project_rand_weighted_err.zip) i sent.
```diff
Random weighted call with array: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
- ERROR: Weight array sum is zero.
Returned index: -1
# other code is still executed and -1 is read as the return value
```

About the second loop: 
As far as my understanding and testing goes it is only utilized when `randf()` returns `1.0` (about 1 in every 4 billion calls).
In these cases (if no floating point imprecision caused something else) `remaining_distance` will be `0.0` on the last `if (remaining_distance < 0) { return i; }` check, thus not being returned.
Instead the index of the last relative likelihood that wasn't zero is returned.
Here an extract from a test of mine to illustrate what happens when `randf()` returns `1.0`
```diff
Random weighted call with array: [0.1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0]
rand_weighted - index: 0, weight: 0.100000, remaining_distance: 1.000000
rand_weighted - index: 1, weight: 0.500000, remaining_distance: 0.500000
rand_weighted - index: 2, weight: 0.500000, remaining_distance: 0.000000
rand_weighted - index: 3, weight: 0.000000, remaining_distance: 0.000000
rand_weighted - index: 4, weight: 0.000000, remaining_distance: 0.000000
# Reached 2nd loop, because remaining_distance is not < 0.0 even on the last iteration.
Returned index: 2
```

Ah I see. Thank you for doing the legwork on that second loop thing, that would've bothered me forever.

As for the main topic at hand, I think I'm still leaning toward warning over error, if for no other reason than to infer that it's "potentially unwanted behavior" over "bad usage" Though full disclosure, I'm biased by my own projects.
I'll go with limiting the commit to it's original scope, any further discussion surrounding zero-array error handling will take place on another pr i will open shortly.
Thanks! Congratulations on your first merged contribution! 🎉
